Chapter 13 · The great schools · 1895–1960

Psychoanalysis and its developments

From Studies on Hysteria to Klein, Horney and Bowlby: what psychoanalysis proposed, why it split and what remains of its ideas today.

While laboratories measured sensations, a Viennese neurologist was treating patients in his consulting room whose symptoms medicine could not explain. From that clinical practice came psychoanalysis: a theory of the mind, a method of treatment and, for much of the twentieth century, one of the most influential ideas in Western culture.

What were people trying to understand?

Why some people suffered paralysis, blindness or anxiety with no apparent physical cause, what part desires and memories we are unaware of play in our lives, and how childhood shapes the adult personality.

With what methods?

Almost exclusively case studies in the consulting room. Josef Breuer and Sigmund Freud published Studies on Hysteria in 1895, describing how symptoms improved when patients talked about painful experiences. One of those patients, Bertha Pappenheim ("Anna O."), called it "the talking cure". Freud gave up hypnosis in favour of free association: the patient says whatever comes to mind without censoring it, and the analyst interprets. He added the analysis of dreams, slips of the tongue and transference, the feelings the patient transfers onto the therapist.

Who took part?

In The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) and later works, Freud proposed that much of mental life is unconscious, that infantile sexuality plays a central role and, from 1923, that the mind is organised into id, ego and superego. Dissenters soon appeared. Alfred Adler gave more weight to feelings of inferiority and to social context. Carl Gustav Jung broke with Freud in 1913 and developed analytical psychology, with the collective unconscious and archetypes.

The next generation shifted attention to relationships. Anna Freud systematised the defence mechanisms (1936) and worked with children. Melanie Klein analysed children's play and founded the object relations school. Karen Horney criticised the Freudian view of women and stressed the influence of culture. The psychiatrist John Bowlby, trained as a psychoanalyst, broke with orthodoxy by studying the real separation of children from their mothers, and attachment theory came out of that work.

What did it contribute?

  • The idea that talking about what troubles us can relieve suffering, the basis of the psychotherapies.
  • The importance of non-conscious processes, which cognitive psychology has studied with other methods.
  • Everyday concepts: repression, projection, denial, defence mechanism.
  • Attention to childhood and early relationships, which links to attachment theory.

What was revised later?

Psychoanalysis was criticised for resting on cases that are hard to verify, and some of Freud's case histories have been re-examined with documents showing that the outcomes were less favourable than he reported. Many of his specific hypotheses, such as a universal Oedipus complex or penis envy, have found no empirical support. Even so, today's brief psychodynamic therapies have been tested in clinical trials with results comparable to other psychotherapies for some disorders, and the existence of unconscious mental processes is now accepted, though in terms very different from Freud's.
